newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican separatists mount 58-bomb show of force.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatists mount 58-bomb show of force.

text.p: Corsican separatist guerrillas defied a French government crackdown to mount a show of force on the Mediterranean island on Sunday, exploding 58 mostly tiny bombs in a few hours.

No one was injured in the pre-dawn blitz and damage was mostly limited to smashed windows or damaged doorways at post offices, tax offices and other symbols of French state authority in towns and villages.

The outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) Historic Wing, seeking to prove it has not been crushed by the detentions of three political leaders in recent weeks, said it planted the 58 bombs and four others that failed to explode.

"The future lies in struggle," it said in a statement, accusing the centre-right French government of betrayal and reiterating calls for greater autonomy for the island. "We will have multiple struggles, both in Corsica and in Europe."

It was the most violent night on the tourist island since February 9 last year, when the Resistenza separatist group staged 50 blasts and attempted bombings. On one night in August 1982, more than 100 bombs exploded.

Police did not report any arrests despite security bostered by police reinforcements from the mainland. The government has pledged to crack down on 20 years of separatist violence on the island of 250,000 people.

Most bombs were in remote rural areas where gendarmes mount only sporadic patrols with one bomb in the main town, Ajaccio. Investigators reckoned 120 to 150 people were involved in the attacks, planting sticks of dynamite with slow-burning fuses.

Corsican guerrillas have never been taken as seriously as Irish Republican Army guerrillas in Northern Ireland or ETA Basque separatists in Spain, partly because they deliberately seek to avoid casualties and are deeply divided over their tactics and goals.
Opinion polls show most people on Corsica, the birthplace of Napoleon, do not want full independence from France but many favour separatist goals of a greater role for Corsican language and culture.
The FLNC Historic Wing's statement denounced the rival FLNC "Normal Wing", for announcing last week that was renouncing violence and would rely on political campaigns to press its goals for autonomy.

The FLNC Historic Wing has staged attacks in mainland France recently. Its statement said it planted a bomb at a post office in the Riviera capital of Nice on Thursday. It had previously claimed a bomb at an Air France office in the town on Tuesday.
Most of Sunday's blasts were in the north of the island.

Many occurred between 4.30 a.m. and 5.30 a.m. (0330 and 0430 GMT), targeting 13 post offices, half a dozen tax offices, state-run banks, chambers of commerce, two Air France offices and other state-run buildings.
Three unoccupied private villas were also damaged. The northern town of Bastia was hardest hit with 15 blasts at state-run banks, a telecommunications office and an office for war veterans.
There were a total of 574 bomb attacks in 1996 and 602 in 1995, but prosecutors say many were linked to organised crime.

Francois Santoni, the head of the FLNC's political wing A Cuncolta, is in police detention on suspicion of involvement in extortion and bomb attacks after giving himself up on December 16. Two other Cuncolta leaders are also in detention.
